source.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
source.authors: Danny Hernandez; Tom B. Brown; Tom Conerly; Nova DasSarma; Dawn Drain; Sheer El Showk; Nelson Elhage; Zac Hatfield-Dodds; T. Henighan; Tristan Hume; Scott Johnston; B. Mann; Chris Olah; Catherine Olsson; D. Amodei; Nicholas Joseph; J. Kaplan; Sam McCandlish

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It reports its own model-size and training-time results bearing on double descent, using repeated-data training in transformer language models rather than the original studies' setups.
record.gate_note: The paper varies model size, repetition frequency, repeated-data fraction, and training time, and reports test-loss outcomes. Cited double-descent results from other studies are not recorded as rows. Values used to fit scaling curves or choose boundaries are not separate outcomes unless the paper reports an outcome for them.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own test-loss results in a new setting: transformer LMs trained on mostly unique data plus a repeated subset. These include epoch-wise learning curves (Fig 3) and model-size effects (Fig 4), which the authors explicitly frame as model-wise and epoch-wise double descent. The setting is new rather than a different method aimed at the original question, so T3 rather than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that a small repeated fraction, at a particular repetition frequency, causes severe degradation (up to about a 2x effective size loss). They describe this as double descent over repetition frequency, model size and training epochs. The degradation scales predictably as a band in the size-by-epochs plane, occurs for text and Python, and coincides with memorization of the repeated subset. It also disproportionately damages copying and induction heads.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains transformer language models on mostly unique data plus a repeated subset, varying model size, repetition frequency, and repeated-data fraction; it does not reproduce the original studies' setups.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome depends on repetition frequency, repeated-data fraction, model size, and dataset: 90% repeated data yields epoch-wise double descent, while 50% yields long plateaus; Python curves are noisier and differ in shape. The authors also state that regularization differences could meaningfully shift the poor-performance region.

fits_no_version.finding: Final test loss peaks at an intermediate repetition frequency for fixed repeated-token share and budget, and the peak shifts with model size. For example, 800M parameters with about 100 repeats of 0.1% of data performs near a 340M model. This holds for text (Fig 2 left, Fig 15), Python (Fig 11) and 1-layer attention-only models (Fig 19).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Repetition-frequency-wise double descent: at a fixed share of repeated tokens, test loss peaks when the repeated subset is just memorizable by the model.

record.problems: The study uses a fixed 100B-token budget rather than a compute-optimal frontier; the fitted poor-performance boundaries are noisy and rely on aggregation and interpolation; the 1% repeated-data scans were noisy and excluded from fits. The paper measures loss rather than downstream NLP evaluations and did not explore early stopping, dropout, weight decay, or other regularization.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted. Results on copying, prefix matching, induction heads, Python out-of-distribution loss, and fine-tuning do not measure the model-size or epoch-wise test-error behavior named by V1 or V2.

untested.parts: Any rise in absolute test error with model size; a peak at the size that fits the whole training set (here the peak tracks memorization of the repeated subset only); settings without a repeated subset; architectures other than transformers.
Training-time curves at 10% or lower repeated fractions; ordinary training without an injected repeated subset; models other than the 800M model.
Not tested: the total training-sample count is never varied near an interpolation threshold.
Not tested: only transformer LMs, including attention-only variants.
Not tested: no single effective-complexity measure is used to predict the peak across axes. The E = k*N^alpha band fit is empirical and limited to the epochs-by-size plane.
Not tested: no label noise is introduced, no multiple peaks are reported, and regularization was not explored (stated limitation 5).
Not tested: the model-size multiplier is a reporting unit, not a recount of effective parameters.

missing.what: The degradation peak coincides with training loss on the repeated subset approaching zero. This bears on where the peak sits relative to fitting (of a sub-distribution, not the full training set).

Per-fraction model-size-multiplier curves against repeated epochs at 1%, 3%, 10% and 50% repeated data. The 1% curves were too noisy and were excluded from the fits; at 3% the maximum degradation is about 1.15x.

record.verdict_notes: The record overstates V1: Fig 4 shows a relative deficit against the scaling fit, not test loss rising with size. R5 and R6 were mislinked to V2 because their x-axis, 'epochs on repeated tokens', varies across runs rather than over training time. Repeated data here is a random subset, not label noise.

versions.untested_parts: The model-size results concern transformers trained with repeated subsets; the paper does not test the claim across arbitrary deep-network settings or identify a conventional training-set interpolation threshold.
The epoch-wise results are for repeated-data training; the paper does not establish that this shape holds for ordinary training without repeated data.
The study varies repetition fraction and repeated-subset size, not the number of training samples near an interpolation threshold.
The paper studies transformer language models, including attention-only variants, rather than a range of model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak location across model size, epochs, and sample count.
The study does not vary label noise or tune regularization to test peak causes or disappearance; it notes that regularization was not explored.

The study uses effective model-size multipliers to express performance loss, but does not test whether counting complexity by effective parameters turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: transformer language models
rows.size_stated: 10M–1B parameters in the described size range
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size at a repeated-data frequency of 1,220 repeats, with 10% of tokens from repeated data; compared test-loss performance with the unique-data power-law scaling fit.
rows.measure: Test loss expressed as an effective model-size multiplier relative to the unique-data scaling fit
rows.value: 0.55x model-size equivalent at 10M to 100M parameters; performance recovers to 0.8x for a 1B parameter model
rows.note: The paper describes a dip and recovery in the effective model-size multiplier as model size increases; this is a repeated-data condition, not a claim of an unconditioned raw-error curve.
rows.check: The measure is an effective model-size multiplier relative to the unique-data power-law fit, not raw test error. The dip from 0.55x to a 0.8x recovery is a deviation from the scaling trend. No rise in absolute test loss with model size is reported (Fig 2 right shows only divergence from the power law). So the fall-rise-fall shape in test error is only partly shown. Recovery is also incomplete (0.8x, not 1x).

source_check.correct: V1 state: cannot_determine. At 1,220 repeats and 10% repeated tokens, the effective model-size multiplier reaches 0.55x at 10M–100M parameters and recovers to 0.8x at 1B. These relative multipliers do not establish an absolute test-loss rise and recovery.
source_check.locator_found: Results, Figure 4 and accompanying paragraph, lines 370–391; Appendix A, lines 1430–1435.
source_check.problem: The relative scaling-law measure cannot establish V1; partial is inappropriate.

rows.subject: transformer language models
rows.size_stated: varied; the dip is described as centered around 1B parameters
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size at 122 repeated-data epochs, with 10% of tokens from repeated data, and measured test-loss performance relative to unique-data scaling.
rows.measure: Test loss expressed as an effective model-size multiplier relative to the unique-data scaling fit
rows.value: The performance dip occurs later, centered around 1B parameters
rows.note: The text locates a dip but does not describe a recovery for this condition.
rows.check: Same relative-multiplier measure as R1. The dip is centred around 1B, the top of the tested range, so recovery cannot be seen. The text also describes this condition as a divergence after 100M, with no absolute loss rise reported.

source_check.correct: V1 state: cannot_determine. At 122 repeats, relative performance diverges from the scaling law after approximately 100M parameters, with the relative dip centered around 1B. An absolute fall-rise-fall test-loss curve is not established.
source_check.problem: A relative performance dip without an established absolute loss rise cannot be classified as partial V1.

rows.subject: 800M parameter transformer model
rows.operation_detail: Measured test-loss learning curves over training time while varying repetition frequency in the repeated subset.
rows.value: For several models, test loss drops, rises during the middle of training, and then drops again
rows.locator: Results, Figure 3 left and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors describe literal double-descent curves in this 90%-repeated-data setting.
rows.check: Correct. Add the condition that the literal fall-rise-fall occurs only at 100x-10,000x repeats, per the Results text.

rows.subject: 800M parameter transformer model
rows.operation_detail: Measured test-loss learning curves over training time while varying repetition frequency in the repeated subset.
rows.value: The double-descent bumps become long plateaus for highly affected models
rows.locator: Results, Figure 3 right and accompanying text
rows.note: The authors characterize this as an epoch-wise double-descent phenomenon, but the reported curves are plateaus rather than a clear fall-rise-fall.
rows.check: Correct as partial: at 50% repeated data the bump becomes a long plateau rather than a rise.

rows.subject: transformer models trained on Python
rows.size_stated: varied; up to 805,000,000 parameters in Figure 11
rows.stage_stated: training on Python; approximately 2 epochs of the dataset
rows.operation_detail: Measured Python test-loss curves over epochs on repeated tokens.
rows.measure: Python test loss over training time
rows.value: The paper reports a double-descent phenomenon; the curve shape differs somewhat from the text experiments and the fit is noisier
rows.note: The authors report double descent in the Python sweep, while noting noisier fits and a different curve shape.
rows.check: Fig 11 plots final Python test loss against epochs on repeated tokens across separate runs; each run has a different repeated-subset size and the same token budget. It is not a learning curve over training time. It shows a peak along the repetition-frequency axis, so it does not measure V2's training-time shape. Its subject should say models trained on Python; the operation is a repetition-frequency sweep.

rows.subject: 1-layer attention-only models
rows.operation_detail: Measured test loss over epochs on repeated tokens.
rows.value: The paper reports that these models also show double descent on repeated data
rows.note: The text explicitly describes double descent; the figure does not supply a numerical summary.
rows.check: Fig 19 plots final test loss against epochs on repeated tokens across runs, not loss over training time. It is a repetition-frequency peak, not epoch-wise double descent. The model size is not stated.

relationships.condition: Transformer LMs, 10% repeated data, 100B tokens, 1,220 and 122 repeats
relationships.reason: The size-wise effect appears only as a dip in model-size multiplier relative to the scaling law (0.55x, recovering to 0.8x). No absolute test-loss rise is reported, and the 122-repeat dip shows no recovery within range (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: The model-size multiplier dipped to 0.55x and recovered to 0.8x without a reported absolute test-loss rise, while the 122-repeat dip showed no recovery.
